The third quarter of 2011 was mixed for the automotive industry. The more developed markets showed a remarkable amount of

vigour. North American car and truck sales and production continued to recover. In Japan, production grew strongly as the industry moved back towards full production following March’s disasters. In Europe, austerity measures and economic concerns both affected consumer demand negatively and car sales fell (though diesel car sales actually increased). European production was healthier as it found support from Chinese consumers interested in buying European luxury models. In the growth markets, however, the story was rather disappointing. Chinese attempts to cool an overheated economy seem to be bearing fruit but have slowed the pace of growth to low single digits in percentage terms, hugely lower than last year’s thirty per cent. Government action in Brazil and high inflation in India have had a negative impact on these markets too with last year’s strong growth replaced by slowly shrinking vehicle sales. We expect growth rates in these three markets to increase again next year. |**Region**|**Share**

However, while sales of new cars have fallen in this region, manufacturing has performed well, aided by exports of luxury cars to markets such as China. Data from the European car market shows the negative impact of the ongoing debt crisis on consumer confidence within Europe: 10.1 million passenger cars were sold in the region during the first nin

e months of the year, a decline of a little over one per cent compared to the same period one year earlier. Interestingly, September sales themselves were marginally up compared to September 2010. However, Portuguese, Spanish, Irish and Italian buyers were less keen to buy new vehicles than they had been one year earlier as austerity continues to bite. While more cars were sold in the small Greek market in September 2011 than in September 2010, year-to-date sales are one third down on the first nine months of last year. 

However, it is worth noting that European Union Jul 07 Jan 08 Jul 08 Jan 09 Jul 09 Jan 10 car sales fell 1.8 per cent year-on-year in October: the downturn is not yet over and the worsening Euro crisis means that sales could still fall further. Austerity in a number of countries will reduce public sector or governmental purchases of new vehicles next year and fragile consumer confidence suggests that the market is unlikely to improve. A number of manufacturers have started to make small cuts to production and to their forecasts for next year. **Consensus forecasts see 2012’s European vehicle output at only slightly higher levels than during 2011, which would be neutral for platinum group metal demand.** 

Production has, though, been stronger than a year earlier due to the ravenous appetite of Chinese consumers for German luxury cars. German production in Q3 2011 was 1.42 million light duty vehicles, less than in Q1 and Q2 but strongly more than in the third quarter of 2010. However, concerns over slowing Chinese growth have recently added to the depression surrounding the European market. While the final months of this year will not be too exciting in terms of the rate of growth of exports of luxury cars to China, this market has grown significantly this year and will grow again next year. Looking further forward, there are some signs that the Chinese Government is succeeding in taming inflation. **If this is true and the Euro crisis does not worsen, then we would expect to see sustained Chinese demand for European cars next year, supporting palladium demand.** 

Within Europe, fleet car sales have become more important in supporting new car demand and, in particular demand for diesel vehicles. According to AID (www.eagleaid.com), an automotive industry newsletter, the European market share of diesel passenger cars climbed to a record 55.2 per cent in the first nine months of this year, roughly four per cent more than was the case last year. The national nature of these markets is illustrated by the fact that three quarters of new cars sold in Belgium are diesel-powered whereas less than a third of new Dutch cars use diesel fuel. 

High fuel prices drove the number of diesel cars sold within the UK higher even as the domestic market for all new cars contracted by five per cent as smaller diesel models started to gain sales. UK September sales were 0.7 per cent lower than in September 2010. However, private car buying slipped by

more than 9 per cent to only 47 per cent of the total market. Over half of the vehicles purchased were bought either as fleet cars or directly by businesses. Fleet sales rose therefore and, as a result, while the number of gasoline-fuelled cars sold in the first three quarters of the year fell from 890,000 units in 2010 to 759,000 units in 2011, the number of diesel cars registered by purchasers rose by 6.4 per cent, 3

This has roughly balanced the impact of further substitution of platinum in diesel catalysts by palladium (Johnson Matthey estimates that 30 per cent of the metal used in European diesel catalysts will be palladium this year, up from roughly 25 per cent last year) and **platinum demand should be roughly flat this year** . In its most recent report on the platinum group metals market, Johnson Matthey estimated that demand for platinum from the European heavy duty diesel manufacturers climbed by 40 per cent to almost 50,000 ounces. The most recent data on this market indicates that it is still growing strongly with sales of commercial vehicles within Europe 7.5 per cent above 2010 levels for the year-to-date. While this market accounts for a relatively small proportion of the total of nearly 1.5 million ounces of platinum used by the European automotive industry in a typical year, **growth in the commercial vehicle sector will continue to support platinum demand.** Looking at the UK again, the existing rules in force within London’s Low Emissions Zone will be tightened at the start of January 2012. Currently, a vehicle meeting Euro 3 particulate emission standards is permitted to enter London without paying a Low Emission Zone charge (although the driver may have to pay a congestion charge zone if they drive into central London). In January, any larger vehicle failing to meet Euro 4 rules will be liable to pay either £100 or £200 per day to enter the Low Emission Zone (LEZ). Roughly a third of the commercial vehicles on London’s roads do not meet Euro 4 standards and the high daily cost of using non-compliant vehicles within London **should boost retrofitting using diesel particulate filters and sales of new commercial vehicles, boosting platinum demand in the short to medium term** . ## **North America** Monthly US light duty vehicle sales, million units

The North American market was significantly healthier in Q3 2011 than had previously been expected. Despite a subdued economy, US light duty vehicle sales were 3.1 million units during the quarter, almost 100,000 higher than in Q2 2011 and 200,000 units higher t

han a year earlier. Passenger truck sales rebounded as oil prices fell and consumers started to revert to more normal buying behaviour as they are forced to replace vehicles which they have clung onto for several more years than they had intended. **This has driven up average catalyst loadings and is positive for palladium demand.** Sales of new passenger vehicles in Canada and Mexico were weaker than in Q2 but slightly higher than a year earlier. More recently, October car sales reached 489,000 units in the USA, five per cent more than a year earlier. Passenger truck sales climbed by 10 per cent to 532,000 units, suggesting that, in the absence of a further economic downturn, **the industry may slowly be moving back towards healthier levels of sales and higher palladium and rhodium demand** . September was the third anniversary of the collapse of Lehman Brothers, marking the worst phase of the initial global economic crisis. Since that point, new car sales and leasing have been depressed. As a result, the availability of used cars, whether previously leased or owned, has been greatly reduced, meaning that used car prices are rising strongly, and new cars have become comparatively more attractive. This situation is likely to persist until at least 2013, providing further support for new passenger vehicle sales. Looking at production figures, 2.11 million light duty vehicles were manufactured in the USA during the third quarter, the best performance since the third quarter of 2008, 4
**Mitsui Global Precious Metals | Pole Position** **01 December 2011** demonstrating the steady recovery of this market. Quarterly output does, though, remain some way below pre-crisis levels when it regularly topped 2.5 million units. Some of this underperformance has been balanced by an increase in Mexican production which has risen by over 200,000 vehicles per quarter during the same period. However, Canadian passenger vehicle production has fallen compared to one year ago, dropping from 498,000 units in Q3 2010 to 443,000 in Q3 2011 as a stronger currency has encouraged a slow shift southwards in output. Looking at the longer term, the diesel engine continues to make steady progress in the North American passenger car market. However, it is important not to get too excited yet: for the first ten months of 2011, US sales were only 82,000 units, or 0.7 per cent of the total market. This was, though, more than 25 per cent above sales for the same period in 2010. Part of this relative success was driven by this year’s launch of the 2012 VW Jetta TDI. A number of the major manufacturers plan to launch a diesel car in this market in either 2012 or 2013 and we believe that this **will encourage additional demand for platinum (and palladium)** in their emissions control systems. ## **Japan** Q3 2011 was generally positive for the Japanese automotive industry despite the fact

that production and sales were lower than in Q3 2010. The first positive signs came as car production rose above August 2010 levels during August 2011. This was the first year-on-year growth in output since September 2010 and marks a return to close to normal levels of production following March’s triple disaster. Total Q3 output was 2.03 million units, only 110,000 units below Q3 2010 but 750,000 vehicles more than were produced in Q2 2011. The full year forecast is for production to be some fifteen per cent below last year’s levels. It would, however, be wrong to assume that production has been fully normalised. Component shortages still persist in some subsectors and output of certain models remains impaired. Until all Monthly Japanese light duty vehicle

vehicle models become widely available once again, sales of Japanese cars are set to underperform compared to their full potential. Looking into Q4, output has already been negatively affected by the Thai floods to add to the challenges of reaching full production once again. Having recovered to close to full output, a shortage of some parts normally manufactured in Thailand forced Toyota to cut its car production by roughly a quarter initially. Output had almost fully recovered by late November. We expect vehicle production within Japan to be at normal levels next year despite economic weakness and a strong Yen, suggesting that **platinum group metal demand will increase next year** . Domestic demand is somewhat disappointing, however. Car sales were weak after March’s triple disaster and are recovering slowly. The share of midget cars (below 660cc in engine swept volume) has increased again, rising to 32 per cent of sales, having fallen back last year to a shade over 30 per cent of the market. Sales of larger low emissions cars were boosted by last year’s subsidy programme which has now ended. With that programme having expired, the most cost-conscious consumers have fallen back to buying these cheaper, smaller cars. **This will limit any increase in average catalyst size and precious metal loading this year.** Although new emissions rules for heavy duty trucks were expected to drive additional sales during 2011, this increase has not arrived. **The truck market is now expected to grow next year instead, leading to a small amount of additional platinum demand in 2012.** 5

October passenge

r car production climbed 5 per cent on October 2010 to 1.25 million units while sales were 1.22 million units, one per cent more than a year earlier. This, though, marks a remarkable turnaround from the breakneck speed of growth in 2010 and reflects the tightening or removal of various subsidy schemes, local government efforts to reduce congestion or pollution, and fears of a slowdown in the Chinese economy in general. Although October sales figures can be misleading due to the week-long National Day holidays, some concerns are now emerging over the health of the luxury car segment too. In mid-September, the Chinese Government announced changes to its environmental subsidy programme for smaller vehicles. These amendments took effect at the start of October. Previously, these subsidies could reduce the purchase price of a new car by up to RMB 3,000 (or roughly US$500). However, a tightening of the eligibility rules means that only the vehicles with the very best fuel economy will now qualify. Previously over 400 different models were included in this programme but this figure has fallen below 40. Many consumers responded logically and brought forward purchases which might otherwise have occurred in early October into September. As a result, we saw relatively healthy sales figures for Q3 in China but expect to see a slowdown in growth in Q4. For the year as a whole, the China Association of Automobile Manufacturers is now expecting growth of below 5 per cent in light duty vehicle sales. However, we feel that it is important to maintain some perspective over this market. Slowing growth _does not_ equate to a decreasing market size. On the contrary, growth is still growth and this market will be a little larger this year than last year. Growth rates have decreased from last year’s remarkable thirty per cent but the number of cars and catalysts manufactured in or for this market should increase. Additionally, **the introduction of China 4 emissions standards (closely analogous to Euro 4 rules) in mid-2011 has increased average metal loadings this year and Chinese automotive palladium demand will rise** (from roughly 975,000 ounces in 2011 to an estimated 1.065 million ounces according to Johnson Matthey’s latest estimates). The picture for 2012 is a little unclear. While any major escalation of the Euro crisis could wreak significant damage on the global economy, the current expectation is that the Chinese domestic economy will grow by something between 8 and 9 per cent. There is an ongoing attempt to limit the “abuse” of official cars and this could restrain growth. Some city or local governments may try to introduce restrictions on car ownership or car usage too but growth of ten per cent o

r more in car sales can be expected next year nonetheless. Looking further forward into the future, recent forecasts by China’s National Development and Reform Commission indicate that Chinese domestic light duty vehicle production capacity could exceed 30 million units per year by 2015. When put in the context of a current global market of roughly 80 million units, this shows the scale of the expansion still expected by some in this key market. Adding in the impact of future emissions control regulations illustrates that **additional further platinum group metal demand can be expected in the medium to longer term** . 6
**Mitsui Global Precious Metals | Pole Position** **01 December 2011** ## **Brazil** For the first three quarters of 2011, Brazilian car sales were 1.55 million units, 3.4 per cent lower than in the first nine months of last year. At the halfway point, they were only one per cent lower than a year earlier so efforts to cool an overheating economy are starting to have an impact. Looking at the light duty vehicle market as a whole (including trucks) gives a more positive picture but also demonstrates this slowdown: 2.07 million units were sold and registered in the first nine months of 2011, an increase of 1.1 per cent on the previous year. At the halfway point of 2011, sales had been 3.9 per cent higher than a year earlier. ### **This slowdown in the Brazilian market is bearish for palladium usage.** The Brazilian Government also moved to increase the IPI tax (essentially a value-added tax) on imported passenger vehicles by 30 per cent from September 2011 until the end of 2012. This move, which looks suspiciously like an import tariff, will not be applied to vehicles built either in Mexico or in the Mercosur/Mercosul region. In the longer term, this tax could draw additional investment in the domestic car industry but in the short term it will be negative for sales. Imports have risen from 16 per cent of the car market in 2009 to 23 per cent this year as the Brazilian Real has strengthened and the imposition of such a tax is a strong negative for the car market, which is likely to contract in the final quarter of the year. **This is bearish for palladium demand in the short term.** ## **India** The Indian automotive market weakened in the third quarter of 2011. Passenger car production has now slipped for two successive quarters from the very high rate of early 2011. For the April to October period, however, output of all vehicles was up by 14 per cent, with healthy orders for commercial vehicles one of the main drivers for this growth. Even in the wider market, though, production fell by 1.8 per cent in October compared to a year earlier. The sales figures show a similar trend with sales of passenger cars sliding lower. High fuel prices, global economic uncertainty and very high inflation have all had a negative impact

on consumers’ desire to purchase new vehicles. **Generally, rising fuel prices have been negative for gasoline car sales and positive for the sale of diesel vehicles, boosting platinum demand at the expense of palladium.** The expectation of a large number of product launches in this market in January 2012, a potential slowdown of inflation, and good prospects for continued growth in the wider economy leads us to a positive outlook for this market in the next twelve year. However, uncertainty over possible Government cuts in diesel subsidy is delaying capital investment in new manufacturing capacity and will trim the maximum potential rate of growth. Rest of the World
